kingdom.summary: This is a green, rooted plant that makes its own food, which puts it in Plantae. Chromista photosynthesizers (kelps, diatoms) are brownish or golden, fungi don't photosynthesize and have chitin walls, and protozoa are mostly microscopic single cells.

options.48222: Chromista includes kelps and other brown seaweeds, diatoms and water moulds. Photosynthetic members use chlorophylls a and c, plus brownish pigments such as fucoxanthin, so they look olive-brown or golden rather than grass-green.
options.47126: Plants are multicellular organisms that make their own food by photosynthesis, using chloroplasts with chlorophylls a and b. Their cell walls are made of cellulose and they store energy as starch. Most are green and rooted in place.
options.47686: Protozoa are mostly single-celled organisms such as amoebae and slime moulds, which feed by engulfing or absorbing food. They lack cellulose walls and chloroplasts and are usually microscopic, though slime moulds can form visible blobs.
options.47170: Fungi (including lichens) cannot photosynthesize on their own; they absorb food from their surroundings. Their cell walls contain chitin, and most grow as networks of thread-like hyphae, showing up as mushrooms, moulds, brackets or crusts.

phylum.summary: A tall, branching plant with roots, leaves and flowers needs vascular tissue to move water and sugars. Liverworts are small non-vascular plants, and green and red algae live mostly in water with no true roots, stems or leaves.

options.50863: Green algae (Chlorophyta) are mostly aquatic, from single cells to sheets like sea lettuce. They share plant pigments but have no roots, stems, leaves or vascular tissue.
options.64615: Liverworts are small non-vascular plants that are either flat, lobed thalli or leafy shoots with leaves in neat rows. Their spore capsules sit on short-lived, translucent stalks and they lack true roots.
options.211194: Vascular plants have xylem and phloem, internal tubes that carry water and sugars, letting them grow tall with true roots, stems and leaves. The large, long-lived plant you see is the spore- or seed-producing generation.
options.57774: Red algae are mostly marine seaweeds coloured red, pink or purplish by the pigment phycoerythrin. They have no vascular tissue, roots or flowers, and are usually found attached to rocks in the sea.

class.summary: The leaves are much-divided and net-veined, and the tiny flowers have 5 petals: dicot features. Monocots have parallel veins and flower parts in threes, lycophytes reproduce by spores, and conifers make cones.

options.47623: Lycophytes (clubmosses, spikemosses, quillworts) have small leaves with a single unbranched vein. They reproduce by spores, often in cone-like tips, and never produce flowers or seeds.
options.47163: Monocots typically have one seed leaf, leaves with parallel veins (often long and strap-like with a sheathing base), flower parts in threes, scattered vascular bundles and fibrous roots.
options.136329: Conifers bear naked seeds on the scales of woody cones and have needle- or scale-like leaves. They never produce flowers or fruit, and most are evergreen trees or shrubs.
options.47124: Dicots typically have two seed leaves, net-veined leaves, flower parts in fours or fives, and a taproot. Their stem vascular bundles form a ring, so woody members can make true wood.

order.summary: Many tiny 5-petalled flowers sit on stalks radiating from one point like an umbrella (an umbel), and the ovary is below the petals: classic Apiales. Ericales mostly have fused bell- or urn-shaped corollas, Fabales have pea flowers and pods, and Caryophyllales include pinks and docks.

options.47181: Ericales is a very diverse order including heathers, blueberries, primroses, balsams and tea. Many members have petals fused into bells, urns or tubes, and in heather relatives the anthers often open by small pores.
options.47123: Fabales are mostly legumes: flowers often pea-like with a banner, two wings and a keel, fruits in pods, and leaves usually compound with stipules. Many fix nitrogen in root nodules.
options.47366: Caryophyllales include pinks, chickweeds, cacti, docks and amaranths. Pinks have opposite leaves on swollen joints and 5 free, often notched petals; many members are succulent or salt-tolerant.
options.48700: Apiales (carrots, ivies, devil's club and allies) have small 5-parted flowers in umbels, an inferior ovary (below the petals) and often divided leaves with sheathing bases.

family.summary: Apiaceae are mostly herbs with hollow stems, sheathing leaf bases, compound umbels (umbels of umbels) and dry fruits that split into two seed halves. Araliaceae are often woody with fleshy berries, while Pittosporaceae and Griseliniaceae are evergreen shrubs from the Southern Hemisphere.

options.51596: Pittosporaceae (cheesewoods) are evergreen shrubs and trees mainly from Australasia, with leathery leaves and sticky seeds in capsules. Only planted in BC.
options.52849: Araliaceae (ivy, devil's club, ginseng) are often woody or prickly, with flowers in simple umbels or round heads and fleshy berry-like fruits.
options.71524: Griseliniaceae is a single genus of glossy-leaved evergreen shrubs from New Zealand and South America, often used for hedges. Flowers tiny, not in compound umbels.
options.48699: Apiaceae: usually herbaceous, often aromatic, with hollow stems, leaf stalks that sheath the stem, compound umbels, and a dry fruit (schizocarp) that splits into two one-seeded halves.

genus.summary: Anthriscus has fern-like, finely divided leaves, white umbels without bracts at the base, and narrow, unwinged fruits with a short beak. Heracleum is giant with broad lobed leaves, Foeniculum has yellow flowers and thread-like leaves smelling of anise, and Lomatium has flattened, winged fruits.

options.53095: Heracleum (cow parsnip, giant hogweed) is very large with broad, coarsely lobed leaves, huge flat-topped umbels, and flat fruits with wing-like margins.
options.53053: Foeniculum (fennel) has yellow flowers and leaves split into thread-like segments, with a strong aniseed smell. Grows in dry disturbed sites in SW BC.
options.55343: Lomatium (biscuitroots, desert parsleys) are mostly low native perennials of dry slopes with yellow, white or purple flowers and strongly flattened, winged fruits.
options.52847: Anthriscus: leaves 2-3 times divided into fine, lacy segments; small white flowers in compound umbels with few or no bracts beneath; fruits narrow and smooth or bristly, with a beak, and no wings.

species.summary: Cow parsley is a tall plant (up to about 1 m or more) with smooth, shiny fruits only 6-7 mm long with a very short beak. Bur parsley has small egg-shaped fruits covered in hooked prickles, garden chervil has fruits with a beak about one-third their length, and shiny anthriscus has leaves glossy underneath.

options.158434: Anthriscus cerefolium: annual culinary herb with smooth fruits whose beak is about one-third the fruit's length, and narrower bractlets than cow parsley. Occasionally escapes from gardens.
options.485932: Anthriscus nitidus: European mountain perennial resembling a large cow parsley, but with leaves strongly shiny on the underside and noticeably enlarged outer flowers in each umbel.
options.52846: Anthriscus caucalis: fruits egg-shaped, about 4 mm, covered in short, thick, hooked prickles. Introduced, mainly in SW BC (SE Vancouver Island, Gulf Islands, Fraser delta).
options.124544: Anthriscus sylvestris: 50-100+ cm, lacy leaves, white umbels in late spring; fruits linear to lance-shaped, hairless, 6-7 mm including a beak only about 1 mm. Introduced from Europe to moist roadsides and field edges in BC.
